answer:
A liveness probe answers one narrow question — whether the process itself is alive and able to make progress — so restarting is the indicated action only for a process-local failure. A shared dependency being unavailable does not answer that question. It is an external condition that a restart cannot repair: the replacement process meets the same dependency, fails the same check, and is restarted again, producing a restart loop that consumes capacity without restoring service (a false positive, not a recovery).

The coupling is also a failure-domain error. A shared dependency fails for every replica at once, so a liveness check that includes it converts one correlated external fault into simultaneous failures of all otherwise-healthy instances. The orchestrator then mass-restarts or ejects them, turning a dependency degradation into a wider outage: warm caches and in-flight work are lost, capacity drops exactly when retries and reconnects rise, and the recovery surge adds load to the still-unavailable dependency. The book states this directly: a shared dependency failure can fail every probe and cause mass ejection or restart, and a liveness endpoint should not restart every healthy process because one shared dependency is unavailable.

The correct separation is startup = initialization complete, readiness = may receive traffic, liveness = must restart. Dependency state belongs in readiness (stop sending traffic, or serve a declared fallback or degraded mode) and in external journey/SLO monitoring, not in process lifecycle. A circuit breaker or bounded timeout around the dependency contains its failure without killing the worker. Keep shared-dependency checks out of liveness, bound probe timeouts and frequency, and require consecutive failures before acting, because probe false positives and shared-dependency coupling are common. A green liveness probe still does not prove readiness, correct routing or a healthy dependency, and exact probe behavior depends on the chosen runtime/version.
